summary:
Adinfinitium: autonomy that lands where missions survive.

The lunar south pole holds the Moon's water ice and is the hardest place on it to land. Adinfinitium chooses where and when to land, flies the descent and sends a rover after the ice, proven first in thousands of simulated missions on real NASA terrain.

Navigator uses NASA LRO LOLA 5 m terrain and NASA/JPL SPICE ephemerides to find the landing cell and date where slope, sunlight and Earth contact line up. Pilot is the onboard brain: a 14.8M-parameter transformer pilot that improves on classic guidance (which always flies as the backup), a hazard network, a sunlight model and an autonomous rover. Dream-RSI keeps the models improving offline, and nothing ships unless it is proven at least as safe.

Results: 98.4% landing success on unseen terrain (classic guidance: 97.7%), 99.6% at our planned landing site, about 9% less fuel in every test, hazard detection 2.6x more accurate than the slope rule, and a rover brain that brings home nearly twice as many rovers as the baseline.

All seven models are open on Hugging Face and the code is on GitHub. Built with Python, PyTorch, JAX, Basilisk, Blender and three.js, with AI coding agents (Claude Code). Our ambition: the most reliable autonomous landing in the world.

Team: Ojas, Nimansh, Tanush, Arnav.

details:
Adinfinitium: autonomy that lands where missions survive.

What it does. At the lunar south pole, the place and the hour of landing decide whether a mission survives. Steep or boulder-strewn ground can tip a lander. The Sun skims the horizon, so a crater rim can be lit for weeks while the floor beside it stays dark. And without a line of sight to Earth there are no commands and no data. Adinfinitium is landing and surface-autonomy software built to make those decisions, and tested in thousands of simulated missions on real NASA terrain before anything flies.

How it works.

  • Navigator picks the landing cell and date. It reads NASA LRO LOLA 5 m terrain of the south pole and uses NASA/JPL SPICE to compute the Sun's and Earth's positions. It scores every candidate on slope, hazards, sunlight and Earth visibility, then flies simulated missions to test the best ones.
    • a learned landing pilot (a 14.8 M-parameter transformer) that only corrects classic ZEM/ZEV guidance, which always flies as the physics backup;
    • a hazard U-Net that maps unsafe ground;
    • a horizon/light model that predicts sunlight;
    • a rover brain that drives to shadowed ice edges and returns before its battery runs out.
  • Dream-RSI lets the models keep improving offline, safely. A new version replaces the old one only if it loses no mission that the current model or the physics backup lands.

Results (paired simulation: every model and its baseline fly identical missions):

  • Lander pilot: at least as safe as classic guidance in every test, ahead in most, and uses about 9% less fuel in every test:
    • 98.39% vs 97.66% landing success on unseen maps;
    • 99.6% vs 99.0% at our planned landing site;
    • 98.1% vs 97.5% on 20 new procedurally generated Moon maps.
  • Hazard model: 2.6× the slope rule's F1 on fresh terrain (0.757 vs 0.292).
  • Light model: cuts horizon error by 21–24%.
  • Rover brain: brings back 1.9× more rovers than the baseline planner (33.7% vs 17.9%).

We publish our weak spots too: the pilot does worse than classic after an engine failure, the hazard model struggles on flat ground, and both learned rover drivers failed.

Benefits and impact. Safer landings, less fuel, and site and date choices made from real terrain and real lighting rather than guesswork. The approach is open: all seven models are public on Hugging Face and the code is on GitHub, so agencies and lander companies can check, reproduce and build on it. Our goal is the most reliable autonomous landing in the world, earned through evidence rather than claims.

Tools.

  • Languages: Python and JavaScript.
  • Models and simulation: PyTorch and JAX for the models and simulators; NumPy, SciPy, SpiceyPy and Rasterio for terrain and ephemeris.
  • Mission simulation: Basilisk and Vizard for spacecraft simulation and replay.
  • Website and apps: Streamlit for the Navigator app; three.js and Motion for the website; Blender for the lander, rover and propulsion-module models.
  • Hardware: trained on an RTX 3050 PC and Apple-silicon Macs.
  • AI use: we used AI coding agents (Claude Code) to help write the software.

What makes it creative.

  • Physics first: a learned pilot that can only improve on physics, never replace it. An untrained pilot flies exactly like the classic controller.
    • held-out maps;
    • a final exam flown only once;
    • brand-new procedural Moon maps;
    • every number published with its source and uncertainty.

What we considered. Safety (a physics backup and a zero-regression gate), honesty (failures reported next to successes, no unsupported claims), real data over invented data, the compute limits of student hardware, and making everything open and reproducible.

Team: Ojas, Nimansh, Tanush, Arnav.
